chad-sokol.text: The thrill of the hunt is alive and well at Costco Wholesale Corp. The Issaquah, Washington-based chain of warehouse stores may feature huge retail spaces and a vast assortment of products overall, but the company puts a major emphasis on offering a culled down selection within each category and on rotating through products regularly to create a treasure hunt mentality. For shoppers of the store’s upscale wine, spirits, and beer section this means new labels are introduced often and it creates a sense of urgency while shopping—buy items as they come in because once they sell out they might be gone for good.

Chad Sokol, Costco’s vice president and general merchandise manager for wine, spirits, and beer, says the treasure hunt is a key factor in the continued strength of beverage sales at Costco. That coupled with a product assortment that skews higher-end while being anchored by a top-notch proprietary label program adds up to multi-billion dollar business. It also keeps Sokol and his team of beverage buyers busy.

“I like to say Costco is almost like a wine club in that our buyers select a good variety of wines from different regions and across a few price points to keep the selection manageable,” Sokol says. “Our members come to Costco because we constantly change our mix of items, which we call our ‘treasure hunt’ experience. There’s always a reason to come back and see what’s new.” For his dedication to offering a well curated assortment of wines, spirits, and beer at Costco, Sokol receives the 2026 Market Watch Leaders Retailer of the Year honor.
Beverage Basics

Sokol has been with Costco for more than 30 years and first took over its beverage division in 2020, when former Market Watch Leader and Retailer of the Year Annette Alvarez-Peters retired. Sokol transitioned to a different department in 2023 but came back as vice president and general merchandise manager for wine and liquor in 2025. Over the course of his tenure with Costco, Sokol has held numerous beverage-related roles, including assistant buyer for wine and spirits in the company’s Northern California region. Today, along with managing wine, spirits, and beer, Sokol also oversees Costco’s candy department, which includes not only traditional candy but also nuts, cocoa, protein bars, and meat snacks. Previously, he’s been a buyer and leader of other food items including frozen and refrigerated goods.

“It’s been an amazing learning experience to be in so many areas of the company and to learn vital buying skills that translate very well into the wine and spirits industry,” Sokol says. “I was recently in Asia on a cashew sourcing trip a week before I was in Bordeaux for the En Primeur campaign.”

Beverage sales remain strong and steady for Costco. In 2020, the most recent drinks data available for the company, Costco’s beverage alcohol sales in the U.S. topped $5 billion, and they’re higher today, though the company declines to release an exact figure. In 2025, Costco’s total net sales company-wide were $269.9 billion, up from $163.2 billion in 2020.

Wine is the category leader both by sales and SKUs, and Costco is committed to having an assortment that skews higher-end. “Costco has always focused primarily on fine wines, and wine SKUs typically make up at least 50% or more of our beverage floor sets,” Sokol says. “We’re continuing to expand our fine wine sets while also focusing on premium spirits. Costco’s focus on wine and spirits has remained relatively the same in terms of the overall business and footprint within our warehouses, although trends have certainly changed with the growth of RTDs and new products.”

Costco operates more than 900 warehouse stores worldwide, spanning 14 countries including the United States. The U.S. is by far its biggest market with almost 650 stores and heavy concentrations in California, Washington State, and Florida. Globally, 535 Costco warehouses sell wine, 385 sell spirits, and 571 sell beer. The stores average 146,000 square feet in size and roughly 4,000 SKUs total. For beverage alcohol, the company overall has thousands of wine, spirits, and beer SKUs, though the typical store only stocks about 200 SKUs. Product assortments vary by region and even store, as Sokol says very few brands are stocked chainwide, with the exception being the company’s proprietary Kirkland Signature label, which offers a range of beverage products across wine, spirits, and beer and is purchased at a corporate level. The lack of pre-set brands across the chain is a major point of differentiation for a company with the size and scope of Costco.

“The vast majority of the department is bought by our local and regional buyers,” Sokol explains, adding that he thinks it’s a great asset. “Our regional buying offices cater the selection of wine, spirits, and beer to each local market. Some warehouses, like Scottsdale, Arizona and Napa, California, have very large wine sets, whereas Washington, D.C. has an expansive spirits set based on their sales.”
Winning With Wine

Wine has long been the focus for Costco’s beverage department, making up 50% of total beverage sales, and the company aims to have offerings across the pricing spectrum. Costco’s Kirkland Signature wines are often among the stores’ most affordable. The brand has myriad varietals, from Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Grigio to Chianti and Bordeaux (Kirkland Signature wines range from $6–$28 a 750-ml. at the Issaquah, Washington store). “We try to have a wide variety of Kirkland Signature wines that reflect multiple regions and appellations,” Sokol says, adding that Costco’s proprietary brand is a gateway to wine for consumers who are less familiar with the category. “We carry close to 40 Kirkland Signature items in the locations that have spirits, wine, and beer. Our Kirkland Signature items are doing very well and typically out-pace the rest of the department in overall growth.” Costco stocks a full roster of brand-name wines too, including labels from domestic producers like Silver Oak, Kendall-Jackson, and Grgich Hills, and international players like Italy’s Santa Margherita and Saracco, New Zealand’s Greywacke, Germany’s Dr. Loosen, and France’s Dom Pérignon ($6–$253 a 750-ml.). These join prestige offerings like first growth Bordeaux, as well as luxury bulk wine collections in California only, such as a nine-bottle set of Duclot Collection’s 2019 Bordeaux ($14,000 for nine 750-ml. bottles) and a 24-bottle historical set of Château Haut-Brion magnums spanning vintages from 1992 through 2015 ($50,000 for 24 1.5-liter bottles).

“Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay dominate our overall sales, but right now Sauvignon Blanc and imported whites, especially Sancerre, are incredibly hot and showing consistent growth,” says Brian Zuhlke, Costco’s Los Angeles regional wine buyer. “Our members are gravitating toward lower alcohol, crisper, and fresher profiles. I’ve increased the space allotted for these wines in my region and I’m adding more offerings to capture demand.”

Bena Ahlberg, Costco’s Midwest regional wine buyer, says that in her area of the country Costco shoppers are willing to experiment. “Many of our members are gravitating toward new wines from familiar labels or even new wine brands they haven’t seen before and can’t find at other retailers,” Ahlberg says. “The treasure hunt atmosphere we create in fine wine offers the flexibility to test new wines frequently and keep members engaged. We’ve had great success with wines that are approachable in both flavor profile and price point.”

A few Costco warehouses with the highest wine volumes have wine stewards in-store to assist shoppers, and some locations also host winemakers and brand ambassadors who set up informational stations—Costco calls them roadshows—on site to bolster brand awareness. However Sokol says that for the most part, the company relies on its knowledgeable consumer base and on in-store signage to relay information. Costco doesn’t offer in-store sampling events in the U.S., though some international units do.

“Costco’s business model in all departments is to have great brands that our members hopefully already know,” Sokol explains. “We rely on wineries and brands to build their awareness so that when people come in they already recognize the label. We also look to bring in gems and unique wines that our members may not know, and then we use signs to display ratings, price, and a brief description. Our regional and corporate wine buyers utilize Wine & Spirits Education Trust programs for training and we collaborate with brand partners for ongoing education.”

Wine is also displayed differently than most other products at Costco. Instead of large pallets and products stacked high, most wine departments feature wooden wine boxes and eye-level displays so shoppers can browse easily. “We’re focusing on expanding the fine wine boxes within most Costco locations and cutting back on full pallet offerings,” Sokol says. “This helps us control inventory and keep the rotations fresh. We’ve recognized that full pallets of too many wines can limit the rotations of new items. We can maximize SKU productivity with a better balance between wooden boxes and pallets, and this helps us focus back on what our core members are looking for. It gets us back to our roots, as Costco set out from the early days with the goal of being known as a fine wine retailer.”
Broad Spectrum

Costco built its reputation as a beverage alcohol retailer on its strong wine assortment, but spirits and beer, including RTDs, are also featured in the stores. Spirits make up about 35% of overall drinks sales, led by Tequila, Bourbon, and Scotch. The stores typically carry about 60 spirits SKUs, including big-name brands like Jack Daniel’s, Jim Beam, Tito’s, Don Julio, Cazadores, Johnnie Walker, and Glenfiddich, and these are positioned alongside a full roster of Kirkland Signature labels. The proprietary brand offers several Tequila expressions, as well as vodka, rum, and a wide variety of whiskies from a Bottled in Bond Bourbon to a High-land Scotch. Kirkland Signature spirits are $16–$80 and range in size from 750-ml. to 1.75-liter bottles, depending on the offering; brand name spirits are $16–$183, not including specialty luxury bottlings that can be priced much higher.

“I consistently hear from our members that they’re surprised to see how many highly allocated wines and spirits are available at their local Costco,” Sokol says. The beverage executive adds that along with the frequently rotating selections in stores, the quality and value found among Costco’s beverage department and among its Kirkland Signature wines and spirits make the company stand out in the retail space. “There’s something to offering a limited number of constantly rotating wines and spirits that keeps the department fresh, exciting, and not too overwhelming,” he says. “We really try to focus on treasure hunt items that over-deliver in terms of value.”

Beer is a smaller player at Costco, averaging about 20 SKUs per store, including seltzers and RTDs. The company offers a handful of Kirkland Signature beer items, like its recent Helles lager and hard seltzer variety packs ($14–$25 a 12- to 24-pack of 12-ounce cans, depending on the package). These join larger players like Bud Light, Coors Light, Heineken, and Corona Extra, and craft offerings like Elysian Brewing Space Dust IPA and Georgetown Brewing Johnny Utah pale ale. White Claw hard seltzer is also available, as is Athletic Brewing non-alcohol IPA (brand name beers start at $10 for a 4-pack of 16-ounce cans and go up to $38 for larger packages).

Costco utilizes its own membership mailing, the Costco Connection magazine, to highlight new products and offer educational information about wines and spirits, and the company’s social media team often posts content high-lighting new products. The company doesn’t offer traditional online sales currently, but it has a partnership with Instacart that allows for same-day delivery on several items, including beverage alcohol in some markets. Sokol says the company is exploring options for online orders to be picked up in store, too.

Costco has two membership levels—Gold Star ($65 a year) and Executive ($130)—and boasts an affluent membership base overall, which further supports its high-end wine and spirits selection. Sokol says that going forward, the company will remain committed to the drinks business and to sourcing top-quality, interesting products across wine, spirits, and beer. Within the next year, for Kirkland Signature specifically, Sokol plans to add more Bourbon labels and new wines from different appellations.

“We’re seeing nice growth across many states and regions as we refocus on fine wines, high-end spirits, and RTDs,” Sokol says. “We have strong growth plans to continue to deliver value and unique items for members. Our focus right now is on offering a continual rotation of new items and categories to keep the treasure hunt experience as exciting as possible. We recognize that the wine and spirits department at Costco is a great driver of foot traffic and we’re looking to expand our selection of fine wines and spirits to keep the department exciting.”

abc-fine-wine-spirits.text: The team behind Florida-based ABC Fine Wine & Spirits knows what it means to create a legacy in the beverage industry. The family-owned and operated business has been serving the central Florida area since opening in 1936 under Jack Holloway’s ownership. Today, ABC has 127 stores scattered from the Florida Panhandle to Miami, and the company recently acquired three stores in Colorado that operate under the Applejack Wine & Spirits banner, marking its first foray outside of Florida.

ABC has been passed down from generation to generation. The store is currently owned by Jack Holloway’s grandchildren Charles Bailes III and Jess Bailes, two Market Watch Leaders who have spearheaded the company’s expansion throughout Florida. Now, the fourth generation of family members, Sean Kelly, Dave Larue, Charlie Bailes, Chris Quarles, and Chad Holloway are spearheading the next chapter of ABC, and they’re focused on growing the company that has been nurtured by the generations before them.

“G4 is heavily focused on expansion outside of Florida,” says Sean Kelly, executive vice president of marketing and operations at ABC and the son-in-law of Charles Bailes III. "G3 has given us the space and motivation to do that.”
For their growth mindsets and dedication to the family business, Sean Kelly, Dave Larue, Charlie Bailes IV, Chris Quarles, and Chad Holloway have been named 2026 Market Watch Leaders.
Wanting The Business

ABC’s story began in 1936, when Jack Holloway opened Jack Holloway’s Friendly Neighborhood Bar in Orlando, Florida. Back then, the space operated as a bar and package store, serving Orlando residents who were just coming back to the beverage scene after the prohibition. Years later, Jack Holloway’s Friendly Neighborhood Bar would become ABC Fine Wine & Spirits and eventually get passed on to his son-in-law, Charles “Chuck” Bailes Jr., and then to Chuck’s sons, Charles and Jess. “My grandfather and my father wanted me to come into business, but they wanted me to want to come into the business,” Charles said when ABC won its most recent Market Watch Leaders award in 2024 for community service. “And so they told me to go interview for jobs, which I did, and get the best job offer that I could. And if I was interested, they would match it.”

This is a sentiment that Charles and Jess have carried over into their own leadership. The brothers encouraged each member of G4 to go work somewhere else before joining the family business so that when they came back, it was for the right reasons. “My mom is part of G3, and she moved to New Orleans to go to college at Loyola. So I didn’t grow up around the business like my cousin Charlie did,” says Dave Larue, who serves as executive vice president of sales and purchasing at ABC. “I went to college in New Orleans, and then decided to go work with the family business. But I was 21 years old, and so my uncles asked me to go work somewhere else first.”

Larue spent a year working for Southern Glazer’s in Chicago, which he says was a rewarding experience. After that year, he returned to work for ABC. But his entrance into the business wasn’t cushioned because of his status as a family member. “The first couple years, I was cleaning toilets, working registers, and stocking shelves,” he recalls. “I worked up from the store side, like Charlie did.”

Charlie Bailes IV, Larue’s cousin and Charles Bailes III’s son, is vice president of human resources and internal distribution at ABC, and like his cousin, he worked somewhere else before coming back to Florida to climb his way up through the company ranks. “I worked for a wholesaler running an off-premise route for a year in Chicago. Then moved back to Florida and started running one ABC store…then a group of stores…then much of the state,” says Charlie.

Sean Kelly had a slightly different experience, as he joined the business after marrying Charles Bailes III’s daughter. “Before I moved to Florida, I had a whole separate career. I used to be an investigative reporter for a TV station in Boston, and then I switched to a corporate communications marketing job in Washington, D.C. When my wife and I moved to Florida, I did some ad agency work and other marketing stuff on my own,” says Kelly. “Toward the end of 2017, my father-in-law asked me to put together a team to do a marketing audit of ABC. So I worked on that project for a couple months, and then he asked me to stick around and implement some of what our recommendations were. I really liked the people and the work. I liked everything about it, really.”
Modernization Plans

ABC has changed quite a bit since G4 came onto the scene. “We’ve consolidated old and tired stores that were originally 200-year-old corner stores to make way for newer, more modern locations in upscale markets,” says Chris Quarles, vice president of real estate for ABC. “We’re now expanding nationwide with inline ABC superstores that are over 20,000 square feet.”

The superstores are ABC’s most recent venture, and at press time the company was set to open its first superstore within the upcoming months. While the average ABC store has been between 10,000 and 12,000 square feet, the new stores will range between 22,000 and 30,000 square feet. Within the year, ABC’s Kelly says they’ll have built five superstores throughout Florida. “We’re providing for the guest who likes a great big store, and we’re also providing for those who want convenience in a more condensed form,” says Kelly. “For us, there’s space for all of it.” E-commerce is another area of focus for G4. While the team had been working on their e-commerce channel for years, the Covid-19 pandemic made it an essential part of the business. “When Covid happened, we had already set a foundation for massive growth so we were able to handle it, fortunately,” Kelly says. “And then I think we maintained a lot of it because we didn’t trip all over ourselves trying to scramble to get ready. We were ready.” ABC’s e-commerce sales have leveled out since the pandemic, but G4 remains focused on technologically advancing the company. “I think it had this huge rush when everyone was forced to stay inside or they were concerned about being around other people. It came down, but it continues to grow year over year. E-commerce is now a major part of the business,” Kelly adds. “It feels like we’ve always had it.”

ABC locations are also getting a technological refresh, with new digital aspects throughout the stores to join other cosmetic changes like taller shelves and brighter aisles. “We’re in year four of ripping out our homegrown IT systems and replacing them with modern technology that prepares for the future including AI,” says Charlie Bailes. “That’s been a huge investment and undertaking.”

“I think the technology has helped bring G4 beyond the previous generation and being able to utilize resources that are helping us target new markets with new guest experience,” says Quarles. The group is focused on continuing on with new innovations in order to improve the customer experience at ABC. These days, change is the name of the game. “The ABC stands for Always Be Celebrating in ads but a lot of people say it’s Always Be Changing and that’s true too,” says Kelly. “You have to change and innovate to keep growing.”
Changing Markets

In a struggling economy, ABC, like most retailers, is fighting to stay relevant to the customer and stay in growth mode. ABC’s revenue was estimated to be between $800–$900 million last year. The makeup of the chain’s revenue has shifted over the last 10–15 years. In 2025, spirits accounted for about 59% of the business. The chain stocks upwards of 1700 spirits SKUs in their stores. Tito’s vodka ($20 a 750-ml.) is one of the best-sellers in the category, although Larue says sales for the vodka titan have softened as the overall vodka category continues to suffer. Alongside Tito’s, Smirnoff ($11 a 750-ml.) and Ketel One ($20 a 750-ml.) are holding their own, and Svedka ($10 a 750-ml.) is “exploding” now that Sazerac is behind it. On the whisk(e)y side, Jameson ($25 a 750-ml.), Crown Royal ($20 a 750-ml.), and Jim Beam ($15 a 750-ml.) are all selling well, while Woodford Reserve ($35 a 750-ml.) is a standout. Finally, Tequila is having a moment at ABC, as it is nationwide. Lalo ($40 a 750-ml.) is a standout and Cuervo ($19 a 750-ml.) is “still a hoss” according to Larue, who does the buying for ABC.

Wine accounts for about 25% of sales at ABC stores, with 1509 wine SKUs in inventory. Top sellers include Veuve Clicquot ($59 a 750-ml.), Woodbridge ($6 a 750-ml.), Kendall Jackson ($12–$18 a 750-ml.), and the entire Josh Cellars line (about $11 a 750-ml.). On the higher end of the price scale, Larue notes, “we have a lot of really successful, higher-end SKUs from the Wagner family. Bonanza does really well, as does Caymus.” Caymus and Bonanza sell for $70 and $20 a 750-ml. at ABC stores, respectively.

Beer makes up just 8% of the business. The store’s best sellers are all recognizable names, such as Michelob Ultra ($27 a 24-pack of 12-ounce cans), Modelo ($30 a 24-pack of 12-ounce cans) and Guinness ($17 an 8-pack of 14.9-ounce cans). RTDs have overtaken a bit of the category’s share, with High Noon ($10 a 4-pack of 355-ml. cans) and Surfside ($9 a 4-pack of 12-ounce cans) leading the charge. The remainder of the company’s sales are made up of cigars, miscellaneous items, and one particularly bright spot: THC beverages. Both Larue and Kelly note that despite ongoing legislative issues, THC beverages are garnering traction at their family of stores, accounting for about 4% of the company’s sales on their own.

“The rise of the category is like nothing I’ve ever seen,” Kelly says. “All generations seem to be buying them now, with the largest being in the 35- to 50-year-old range, and a lot of women in particular.”

In an effort to help save the burgeoning category, Larue and Kelly have gotten involved in trying to strike down the ban on THC beverages in Florida. “Dave and I work very heavily on the federal legislation for THC beverages,” Kelly adds. “We’re some of the founding members of a national coalition of retailers working to save THC beverages. There’s a ban coming in November, so there’s enormous effort and strategy involved in trying to preserve the category.” At ABC, Buddi ($12 a 4-pack of 12-ounce cans), and Pamos ($19 a 4-pack of 12-ounce cans) sell well.
On The Horizon

Looking ahead, the members of G4 say there is more expansion on the horizon. Historically a Florida-based company, ABC completed its acquisition of Applejack Wine & Spirits in Colorado earlier this year, marking the company’s first venture outside of the Sunshine State. And according to G4, Colorado is just the first new locale ABC is hoping to enter in the coming years.

The fourth generation also says their focus now is nurturing the legacy G3 is leaving behind while also ushering in a new era that will lay a strong foundation for G5. “If it weren’t for G3 and their contributions, we have no legacy,” says Charlie Bailes. Quarles adds, “Something I have learned over the years is being methodical and having a plan of action for the direction of the company.”

Ultimately, there is a core value the generations share: the responsibility to do right by their employees, their community, and each other. “We are doing our best to represent our family and 90 years of ABC team members in a way that honors their dedication to our stores, each other and the communities we serve,” says Kelly. “We have a responsibility to be great stewards of the ABC brand and the industry as a whole.”

mike-fisch.text: Growing up with Gary Fisch as a father, Mike Fisch always planned to join the family business. Gary Fisch, the president and CEO of Gary’s Wine & Marketplace, launched his first beverage alcohol retail store in 1987 in New Jersey. Thirty-seven years later, in 2018, Mike joined the company on a part-time basis, transitioning to full-time in 2020. Mike Fisch, who has been chief financial officer since 2023, brought financial acumen and a flair for technology to the business, updating systems and introducing technologies that are now being rolled out to the broader industry.

Fisch says he and his dad “make a really great duo” who together are evolving Gary’s Wine & Marketplace to meet the needs of a new generation. “It’s an honor to work with him,” Fisch says. “I value the autonomy and the fact that we focus on parallel things. He focuses on the buying and merchandising, and I focus on the back-office, marketing, technology, systems, and processes.”
For his dedication to family legacy and focus on furthering technological growth at the company, Mike Fisch has been named a 2026 Market Watch Leader.
Early Introduction

Fisch’s first experiences in his father’s retail stores date back a few decades. “The first experience I can remember was handing out lollipops to customers as they walked through the door,” Fisch recalls, noting that he was likely five or six years old at the time. As a teenager, he worked as a cashier and sometimes on the sales floor.

Education and a bit of outside experience was important to Fisch. He studied economics and accounting at Washington University in St. Louis, then joined accounting firm Ernst & Young. A few years later he earned a Master of Business Administration from the Wharton School at University of Pennsylvania.
Earning the MBA “was important to me,” Fisch says, “just to have a bit more legitimacy before I joined the family business so that people knew I was coming in with my own set of ideas and experience.

“It was during my time at Wharton when I started actually dipping my toes into working with Gary’s,” Fisch continues. “I was working on introducing a mobile app to Gary’s and working on our business intelligence reporting and our last mile delivery logistics.”

Those tech developments would become crucial in 2020, when the pandemic upended the business. “Soon after I became full time, Covid-19 hit and we had tens of thousands of people downloading the mobile app because that was the only way to order,” Fisch says. “I got thrown right into the fire and was really able to introduce great systems for the business.”

Now, most of the business at Gary’s Wine & Marketplace has shifted back to in-person, but online makes up about 20% of sales, compared to about 8% pre-pandemic. “It grew the pie because we were able to maintain our in-store sales but also increase our online business,” Fisch says. “People know that they can order on an app, they can order for delivery, they can order for pickup and we have shipping throughout the U.S.”
Business Evolution

Fisch officially joined the family firm in 2018, the same year that his father Gary was named the Market Watch Leaders Retailer of the Year. At that time, Gary’s Wine & Marketplace had five locations—four in New Jersey and one in Napa Valley, California—and about $53 million in annual revenue. In subsequent years, the father-son team opted to close the Napa Valley location and sell another store.
Today, there are three Gary’s Wine & Marketplace stores—in Bernardsville, Closter, and Madison, New Jersey—which together bring in annual revenue of about $48 million, Fisch says.

The moves were made to “really focus our attention and refine our operation,” he adds. “We’re hyper-focused on staff training and staff education. We’ve got an excellent wine team that we send on trips throughout the world to learn and bring back interesting stories and wines to our stores. We’re super focused on in-store experiences and engaging with our community—we want our store to be the cultural hub of our community. Then on the ops and systems side, we’ve just continued to refine and upgrade all our systems so that we can do more with less.”

Those three stores range from 8,000 square feet to 16,000 square feet. Together, the three stores employ about 95 people, of which about 40 work full-time and some of whom have been with the company since its launch 39 years ago.

Within the stores, shelves are packed with wines selected from all over the world, spirits, beer, ready-to-drink beverages, and THC beverages, as well as deli items and gourmet foods. Fisch acknowledges a “moment-in-time softening of purchasing across the industry” but says Gary’s Wine & Marketplace “has been able to buck the trend” for now.

“Offering interesting new products that are sparking discovery is a good way to engage with that next generation, which is where I think a lot of the softening has happened,” he says. “Gen Z, I think, wants to hear about stories. We try to foster that community learning environment and not be relegated to a marketplace app where it’s just a point and click. That’s not where we differentiate. We differentiate on our service and our education [approach]. We want to play to our strengths.”

Currently, Gen Z is gravitating away from wine, but Fisch says he “wouldn’t call it a game” quite yet. “There’s an opportunity for us, as an industry, to pique the interest of those younger consumers,” he says. “We could be one viral video away from everyone wanting to try the next ‘other’ European white wine or whatnot. The verdict is still out.”

As for the overall beverage alcohol sector, Fisch says Gary’s isn’t feeling the squeeze the way some retailers are. Sales increased in 2025 and were pacing flat this year. “We think in this market, that’s actually really good,” he says.

Gary’s stores are strategically located in affluent suburbs with easy access to New York City. Typical customers aren’t particularly price-sensitive, Fisch says, and thus far haven’t shifted their consumption patterns to a great degree despite the faltering economy.
Wine Dominance

For Gary’s, wine has always been, and remains, the focal point. Gary Fisch started the business as an outlet for his passion for wine, and that commitment has held steady for nearly 40 years. “Wine is about 65% of the business,” Mike Fisch says. “It’s what we do best, it’s what we know best, and it’s where a lot of our focus goes.”

Gary’s Wine & Marketplace has about 3,800 SKUs of wine, and buyers are always seeking to add fresh, unique offerings to the curated selection of the wine industry’s finest brands. “Right now, there is a lot of excitement with ‘other whites,’” Fisch notes. “People are exploring lesser-known varieties and wines from Croatia, Greece, and Austria.
“We also see rosé continuing to perform well, despite some talk in the trade about it cooling off,” he adds. “Our numbers are telling a different story.”

About 20% of the wines sold at Gary’s are private labels sold through the company’s Gary’s Direct program. “We find and source these wines, and of course clear them through the appropriate channels,” Fisch notes. “It’s been great for both our customers and our staff. A lot of our internal education is focused on coaching them, teaching them about the interesting Gary’s Direct wines that we discover and bring in. It’s also a differentiator for us to stand out from our competition nearby, because we’re finding wines that are harder to find, are more unique, and our team is passionate about.”
Gary’s Direct wines are sold under a variety of labels and are merchandised as Gary’s Direct offerings in stores. The Fisch family also has its own range of wines within the program.

Spirits are the second-largest category after wine at Gary’s, accounting for about 19% of revenues. With just over 1,800 SKUs, Gary’s spirits offering is comprehensive. Like many retailers, the spirit of the hour at Gary’s is Tequila. “Tequila continues to be the standout category in spirits in terms of driving growth,” Fisch says, noting that super-premium and ultra-premium brands, in particular, are faring well. “And I would say flavored agave spirits is actually an interesting exploration area for certain customers. There are a lot of innovations in that area that I think are exciting.”
Fisch adds, “Spirits-based RTDs brands are certainly still doing well. They’re up 12% year over year for us. We’re carrying about 300 different SKUs, up from 270 last year.”

Beer is a weaker point for Gary’s currently. The chain carries just over 2,000 SKUs for beer, but there’s not much dynamism in the sector other than the continuing expansion of non-alcoholic beers, Fisch says. Beer currently makes up about 9% of business but eating into beer’s share are RTDs and CBD/THC beverages, both of which have growing appeal.
Tempting Experiences

The spirit of exploration extends throughout the stores. In-store events are a critical part of the Gary’s experience. “We invest in in-store experience with frequent sampling events and wine dinners and engaging with the community,” he says, noting that the company typically hosts 30–40 sampling events each month across the three stores. “Every Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, at the very least, we want the stores to be activated.”

Wine tastings and more elaborate dinners are a mainstay of the Gary’s offerings. But it’s not just wine. Tastings can span all categories, including relative newcomer THC/ CBD. “THC/CBD has been a big growth area for the business and something that our customers want to discover and learn more about,” notes Fisch. “It’s an area where we find sampling intrigues customers and will have them buying more than they otherwise would have.”
To manage the thrum of events across the chain, Fisch created a sampling platform called Samplii. That platform is now being rolled out to the broader industry.

Samplii is a way to bring together all different stakeholders in the industry—tasting agencies, distributors, suppliers and retailers—onto one platform. The system increases both efficiency and transparency, Fisch says. “For retailers like Gary’s, we were able to four-times the number of events that we [could before] just by having a booking platform and sending it out to all of our distributor sales reps and all of our suppliers, saying, please book events with us,” he says. “We were able to fill up our calendar and keep it filled up for months in advance.”

In May, one month into the rollout, Samplii had seven retailers and four brands involved. “We’re having really interesting partnership conversations and we think we can bring thousands of retailers onto the platform,” Fisch says.
Future Moves

In fact, Fisch is seeking to extend his reach in the industry beyond Gary’s Wine & Marketplace. The first avenue is expanding Samplii. The second is a consulting business. “I’m taking the learnings from Gary’s—everything we’ve done so far in terms of operations, finance and accounting—and offering those services to other businesses in the industry,” he says. For Gary’s specifically, Fisch says there’s no imminent expansion but opportunities could arise. “The market is turbulent and other players might not be able to maintain market share,” he notes. “It could be a good opportunity for us to buy a company or expand.”
But top priority now is ensuring Gary’s is positioned for continuing success. “A lot of our focus is refining our existing stores and cementing them as staples in the community,” Fisch says.

meghan-cimini-jones.text: As a second-generation beverage alcohol retailer, Meghan Cimini-Jones fondly recalls growing up in the business, acknowledging how it has shaped her career, and making her hopeful that the roots of the family business will continue to grow deep. “I remember riding around the warehouse on beverage delivery U-boats as a kid,” says Cimini-Jones, majority owner of Sturbridge, Massachusetts-based Yankee Spirits, with four stores in the Bay State. The daughter of former Yankee owner Don Cimini, she recalls helping out at one of her father’s stores at a young age. “It was the coolest place. There were penny candy jars everywhere, and I would run up and down the aisles.” Flash forward to 2026 and the working mother of four young children can’t help but notice how things have come full circle. “I now see my kids riding on the U-boats,” she says. “It’s very special.”

Yankee Spirits has been long established as one of the largest and most innovative beverage alcohol retailers in Massachusetts. Don Cimini and partner Mike Muratore purchased the then two-unit chain in 1989, and were both named Market Watch Leaders in 1996. Michael Cimini, Meghan’s brother, then acquired Muratore’s share in 2002, and he was named a Leader in 2009. An ownership dispute, however, resulted in the younger Cimini relinquishing his interest in the company in 2010. Don Cimini passed away in 2013.

“Family businesses can be difficult because of the relationships, but one of the great things is that it has allowed me to perform basically every role at Yankee Spirits,” says Meghan, who has been a constant presence at the stores for decades. From stocking bags at the register and moving empty boxes to the front of the store as a child—earning $1 an hour—Cimini-Jones has worn many hats at the chain, serving as a cashier, front-end manager, auditor, and buyer. “Yankee was my first job,” she notes. “When I turned 18, I would work at the stores on weekends,” and after college, she joined the business full-time, first working under her brother and then under her father. Today, she has general oversight of the four stores and oversees the chain’s online sales and delivery functions.

For her vast experience and commitment to ensuring the longevity of a family-owned retail business, Meghan Cimini-Jones joins her father and brother before her and has been named a 2026 Market Watch Leader.

Yankee Spirits operates four generally large footprint stores—ranging from 20,000 square feet to 28,000 square feet—in Sturbridge, Attleboro, Norwood, and Swansea, Massachusetts. With annual sales revenue in excess of $60 million, the chain employs about 200 workers. Spirits account for 43% of the business, followed by wine at 36% and beer at 22%.

Some 5,500 spirits SKUs are offered, priced from $1 a 50-ml. up to $5,000 a 750-ml. of Macallan 30 Year Double Cask. Bourbon and Tequila are showing the most strength among spirits categories, Cimini- Jones says, while ready-to-drink (RTD) brands are rapidly expanding. Yankee takes great pride in its store barrel picks and customers have responded enthusiastically. “We continue to see a lot of success with single barrels at our stores,” she says. “Our customer base trusts us to make a pick. We’re so selective and we stay very involved in the process to make sure the bottles are exactly what we want.” Indeed, the company strives to be the first in the state with a particular brand, the retailer reveals. Among some of the chain’s most successful single barrels are those from Penelope Bourbon, Copper & Cask, Green River Distilling, and Rare Character Whiskey Co.

“Tequila is also making a strong push,” Cimini-Jones says. And the chain has responded, investing in a wider selection. Top performers include Don Julio Añejo ($58 a 750 ml.), Tequila Ocho Reposado ($55), and Lunazul Añejo ($24). And as at other stores, RTDs are increasingly gaining space at Yankee Spirits. “We’ve reallocated space to make room for RTDs,” she notes, including in the vodka aisle. Top-selling RTDs include High Noon ($19 an 8-pack of 12-ounce cans) and Sun Cruiser ($15). Overall, Tito’s Handmade vodka ($20 a 750 ml.) is the top-selling spirits brand at Yankee Spirits. The stores stocks more than 7,000 wine SKUs, priced from $3 to nearly $1,000 for the 2013 Lucien Le Moine Montrachet. Wines priced between $12 to $25 are the stores’sweet spot, but California Cabernet Sauvignons priced at $35 to $60 are strong performers. Top-selling labels include Kendall-Jackson Vintners Reserve Chardonnay ($12) and Josh Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon ($14). A long-established wine futures program aids the chain in staying on top of consumer interests, Cimini-Jones says. “Wine futures help us with seeing the pulse of where the wine industry is,” she remarks. While the retailer concedes that like other wine shops, Yankee has seen an overall decline in wine futures, she adds that the program “helps us to see what consumers are interested in and what’s moving.” Customer interest in the futures program alone—even if diminished from previous years—is enough to ensure that its continuance is worthwhile, the retailer notes.

The chain offers about 3,000 beer SKUs, priced from $6 a 6-pack to $279 for a 750 ml. of Samuel Adams Utopias. While top sellers include Michelob Ultra, Bud Light, and Heineken, ($14–$17 a 12-pack of 12-ounce cans), Yankee is known for its vast craft beer selection, which accounts for 40% of the chain’s beer sales. Cimini- Jones says the stores take great pride in “working with our customers to have and to bring in the products that they want.” While it’s unlikely a grocery store will go to great efforts to respond to a single customer request, she says, “it happens every single day at Yankee Spirits. We listen to our customers. We also stay connected and follow the trends.”

Indeed, excellent customer service is a mainstay at Yankee Spirits. Each location is staffed with a wine, spirits, and beer consultant to respond to specific customer requests and needs. “Our management team is top tier and constantly working to improve things,” Cimini-Jones says. Other company principals include Jim Juliano, president and corporate spirits director, and Liz Higgins, director and corporate wine buyer. Joe Santos serves as district manager and corporate beer buyer. Members of the leadership team are in constant communication, Cimini-Jones says.

The company’s emphasis on e-commerce and delivery is an extension of its commitment to good customer service. While online sales were established prior to the pandemic, Cimini- Jones notes that e-commerce sales skyrocketed earlier in the decade. Today, they account for about 7% of sales. Yankee has long offered its own delivery of large orders throughout much of Massachusetts, but earlier this year the chain began partnering with Door Dash for on-demand delivery in the Norwood area. “It’s part of our mantra to be all things to all people,” the retailer explains. “We’ve seen a reluctance among the younger demographic to drive to the stores so we’re trying to meet their needs,” Cimini-Jones remarks. “It seems like the natural next step.”

As part of its focus to appeal to all demographical groups, Yankee Spirits utilizes a mix of platforms to advertise and promote its stores. Traditional forums such as billboards, print and direct mail, as well as radio, are part of the mix, as are digital and social media, including Facebook, Instagram, and even a little “dabbling” with TikTok, the retailer notes. With the Sturbridge and Attleboro stores located “off the beaten track,” and with younger consumers not interested in driving far to shop, social media and on-demand delivery help the chain to meet its customers where they are. A new Yankee Spirits website launched this year on June 1.

Cimini-Jones is particularly proud of Yankee Spirits’ full schedule of large-scale tastings, such as customer appreciation events, Bourbon raffles, and grand tastings, not to mention frequent in-store tastings at all four stores. “I love putting on a big show and seeing how grateful our customers are,” she explains. “It’s great to be able to give back to our customers.” Typically free to customers, the tastings often benefit local organizations, thanks to customer donations that Yankee Spirits solicits at the events. A recent allocated Bourbon raffle, for example, raised $9,000 for the Attleboro Fire Department. Among other organizations that the chain regularly supports is St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, as well as local organizations in the communities in which it operates.

While overall beverage alcohol sales may be languishing these days, Yankee Spirits continues to position itself for change. The chain is increasingly adding food items to its stores, with cheese coolers now available at all locations. Holiday gift baskets are also a growing part of the business, Cimini-Jones says. No new stores are currently planned but the retailer reveals, “we’re always keeping our eyes and ears open.” Store renovations are ongoing, she adds, to best reflect changing consumer demand for various products. Despite the downward trend the industry is experiencing, Meghan Cimini-Jones is “hopeful that the industry will soon be looking at brighter days,” she says. “I’m looking forward to a long career in this industry and evolving along with it.” And she’d love nothing more than for her children to also experience the enjoyment and rewards of beverage alcohol retailing. “I’ve always said that this business is my dad’s legacy for my children,” Cimini-Jones says. “I hope that the same pieces remain in place to provide for that.”

fresh-market.text: In just a little more than two years, the beverage alcohol category at The Fresh Market specialty grocery chain has been transformed from one experiencing declining consumption to a segment seeing year-over-year weekly sales growth. The change in course can be credited to the category’s new leadership team which, through a combination of vast experience in both wine and fashion retailing, is spearheading a push to make beverage alcohol as much of a destination for its customer base as are many of its gourmet food departments. Already, the inroads are getting noticed.

“I enjoy turning a vision into a reality,” says Olivier Kielwasser, adult beverage director at the 172-unit chain, based in Greensboro, North Carolina. Indeed, with nearly 30 years of experience in beverage alcohol retailing and a reputation for masterful merchandising, Kielwasser is uniquely qualified to lead the category. Shortly after joining the Fresh Market in 2024, he brought on Kristen Bennett— herself with numerous years working as a retail buyer—as retail category manager. Together, Kielwasser and Bennett are making tweaks to product selection to best appeal to changing consumer interests while expertly merchandising brands both inside and outside the stores’ beverage alcohol section.
For their quick success in achieving desired results during a challenging time for the industry, Olivier Kielwasser and Kristen Bennett have been named 2026 Market Watch Leaders.
The Great Turnaround

This isn’t the first time Kielwasser has been recognized as a Leader. He also received the distinction in 2008 when he served as senior director of beer, wine, and liquor at Ohio-based Giant Eagle supermarkets. (He additionally received the Leaders Best Merchandising award in 2011.) Following that position, Kielwasser worked as director of wine at Sam’s Club and then as wine category lead at BevMo.

Since first getting involved in wine and beer retailing in 2000 at hypermarket Auchan Retail (which no longer operates in the U.S.), Kielwasser has enjoyed “the constant challenge and the discovery of new items and trends,” he says. The retailer also appreciates the social component of the business. “I enjoy the interaction with supplier partners and our customers,” he says. But Kielwasser is most proud of the guidance and support he’s able to lend to his co-workers. “I’m proud of the continuous development of the people on my team,” he says, pointing to Bennett, who also oversees all non-alcoholic adult beverages. “Non-alcoholic adult beverage sales are up over 100% year over year at the Fresh Market,” he reveals. For her part, Bennett says that while her role at the Fresh Market is in its early stage, she’s most proud of launching the chain’s THC beverage program. “I fast-tracked the category when I joined the company, launching it in seven states, rolling it out, and keeping on top of state regulations” she explains, noting that, like beverage alcohol, the THC landscape is constantly changing. “Seeing the response from guests and store employees has made me proud that I launched it. It’s brought in new guests. People at the company are now talking about adult beverages again.” Prior to joining the Fresh Market in 2024, Bennett served on the spirits buying team at Total Wine & More, having previously worked with Family Dollar and in the fashion industry. Within adult beverages, she most enjoys “the stories behind the brands,” Bennett says. Whether it’s Bourbons, non-alcoholic beer, or THC, “many of these stories are very inspiring,” the retailer explains.

Both Bennett and Kielwasser note that the beverage alcohol category is particularly challenged these days, requiring a vigilant eye on consumer buying trends and product performances. Bennett points to “the health-conscious mood of younger demographics” and the impact of GLP-1 medications on the category. She believes that’s why THC drinks and non-alcoholic adult products are succeeding today. “Consumers are drinking less so that’s why we’ve seen those two categories boom,” Bennett says. Kielwasser, meanwhile, cites the upheaval that major distributor moves are having on the business. “The consolidation in the distributor tier and the fact that brands are moving from one distributor to another has resulted in a very fragmented industry,” he says.
Best Grocery Store

The Fresh Market was founded in Greensboro more than 40 years ago by former 7-Eleven executive Ray Berry and his wife, Beverly, as an ode to the charm of European food markets. By 2010, the concept expanded rapidly to multiple states and became publicly owned. Six years later it was acquired by Apollo Global Management, the asset-management company. Then in 2022, Chile’s Cencosud S.A. acquired a majority stake in the Fresh Market. Last year, the South American retail giant purchased the remaining shares in the chain.

The stores’ farmer’s market approach to retail has proven popular with U.S. consumers. In 2025, USA Today’s best readers’ choice awards named The Fresh Market the “best grocery store in America,” also citing its bakery, deli, produce, and prepared food departments. Cencosud doesn’t report the Fresh Market’s annual sales revenue nor break down dollar sales by category. Today, the chain operates 172 stores across 22 states, stretching from Massachusetts to Oklahoma. While there have been recent store closures, Cencosud still sees opportunity for new locations. In the first quarter of this year, four new Fresh Markets were unveiled, including two in the Miami area, which brought the chain to more than 50 stores in Florida.

When it comes to beverage alcohol, wine is the big leader, according to Kielwasser, accounting for 73% of total adult beverage sales, followed by beer and THC at 25%, and spirits at 2%. Wine is available in 151 locations across 15 states. The average store offers around 600–700 wines, priced from about $15–$50 a 750-ml., with the sweet spot around $18. These days, white wines and sparklers are the best performers, Kielwasser says. Top-selling labels include LaMarca Prosecco ($18 at the Greensboro store), Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label Champagne ($71), Whitehaven Sauvignon Blanc ($19), and Kendall-Jackson Vintner’s Reserve Chardonnay ($16).

In addition to branded wines, the Fresh Market sees growing opportunity for private label or “winery direct” and “direct import” selections. Under the Curious Drop label, for example, Asolo Prosecco Superiore DOCG ($17) launched earlier this year while Paso Robles Cabernet Sauvignon ($17) and Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon ($35) were scheduled at press time to be unveiled in August or September. Additional launches are also planned.
Imported Beer Opportunity

Beer is sold in 161 Fresh Market stores across 19 states. The stores offer between 250–400 beer SKUs, with 6-packs generally priced from $9 to $16. Top-selling brands include domestic brews like Michelob Ultra ($18 a 12-pack of 12-ounce cans) and Miller Lite ($14), Bennett says, but imports also get a big focus. Import-style brands like Peroni ($12 a 6-pack of 12-ounce bottles) and Stella Artois ($12 a 6-pack of 11.2-ounce bottles) have experienced “a sudden resurgence in the last few months,” she says, while Guinness ($12) is another brand that’s growing. Bennett sees opportunity to specialize in niche beer imports, given its reputation for gourmet and European-style foods. “We want to be a destination for imports,” she says.

Due to state regulations, The Fresh Market only sells spirits in ten grocery stores in Illinois, Louisiana, and Massachusetts, in addition to a singular full-fledged wine and liquor store in Florida. Between 100 and 200 SKUs, excluding RTDs, are typically stocked at the groceries, with an average price of $24 a 750-ml., Bennett says. Top-selling spirits brands include Tito’s Handmade vodka ($21 at a Chicago store), Hendrick’s gin ($39), and Surfside ($19 an 8-pack of 12-ounce cans).

The 7,000-square-foot Ponte Vedra Beach, Florida liquor store opened last year and according to Kielwasser, “response has been very enthusiastic. We’re seeing some nice growth coming from that store.” Located adjacent to a Fresh Market grocery store, the liquor store boasts about 1,600 spirits and more than 2,500 wines. While there aren’t any current plans to open additional liquor stores, the chain sees potential to further expand with local spirits brands in some markets. Pointing to the success the Fresh Market has had promoting locally produced items in other categories around the store, Bennett says there’s potential to do the same with home-grown spirits in some of its Louisiana and Illinois stores.

Earlier this year, The Fresh Market unveiled another new concept store that highlights adult beverages. To comply with Pennsylvania regulations, the chain opened a Pittsburgh store with an on-premise license to sell beer, wine, and spirits-based RTDs. “It’s huge for us,” Bennett says of the ability to sell adult beverages for both on-site and off-site consumption in the Keystone State, adding that guest feedback has been “very positive.” The store features a bar serving up four draft beers and four wines by the glass. While there are no immediate plans to extend the service to other Pennsylvania stores, Kielwasser says the concept could be considered for future renovations.

In addition to beer and spirits, Bennett oversees adult non-alcoholic beverages at the Fresh Market, which, she says, are thriving. Non-alcoholic brews are particularly performing well, she notes, led by the Athletic brand ($12 a 6-pack in Greensboro) and Best Day Brewing products ($11). THC beverages, meanwhile, are sold in seven states. After adding numerous NABs and THC products in the last year, she says, “We’re now interested in seeing what guests are choosing and growing those products.”
Cross-Merchandising Master

While the stores vary in size, according to Kielwasser, the current new Fresh Market prototype dedicates nearly 1,900 square feet to adult beverages. “In addition, we cross-merchandise wine in a number of out-of-department locations,” he notes, including produce, cheese, floral, and meat and seafood. Innovative displays also highlight wine and beer such as the ongoing “90 Points for Under $20,” which features brands like Pine Ridge Chenin Blanc + Viogner ($13).

With so much accomplished in just two short years, Kielwasser and Bennett aren’t planning any major changes to the Fresh Market’s beverage alcohol department aside from the addition of more non-alcoholic and THC beverages, niche beer imports, private label wines, and local spirits. Their focus will continue to be ensuring that the best possible product selection is available to their guests, while employing convenient and innovative merchandising practices to grow category sales.

mark-pinho.text: Mark Pinho says he is “a passionate wine drinker and collector, but there was no burning desire to jump into wine retail.” Nevertheless, Pinho jumped, becoming CEO of online retailer Wine.com in 2024. “There was a change of control at Wine.com, and the new ownership wanted to make a clean break and try some new things,” Pinho says.

Now, Pinho is leading the charge to shake things up in the nearly three-decades-old company. Wine.com launched in 1998 as eVineyard, a small firm based in Portland, Oregon. In 2001 the name changed to Wine.com. It scaled rapidly over the next two decades, becoming the largest online-only wine retailer in the U.S. In 2018 the company received $32.5 million in funding from Goldman Sachs, and in 2019 Wine.com began selling spirits.

The company thrived during Covid-19 and in 2022, founder Michael Osborn and then-CEO Rich Bergsund were named Market Watch Leaders. Pinho took over in October 2024, and is shifting from a “growth at all costs,” strategy.

Today, Wine.com generates revenue in the mid-$100 million range, a lower number than in recent previous years due to the shedding of most lower-priced wines from its offerings. “Our focus has been on long-term sustainability, so revenue right now is a moving number,” Pinho says.
For his new vision leading the well-known online retailer, Mark Pinho has been named a 2026 Market Watch Leader.
Customer Focus

“One of the things Wine.com was never great at was building customer relationships,” Pinho says. “There’s a convenience factor of just being on the internet, but as we all know, there’s a lot that goes into developing relationships with wine buyers over time.” The purchaser is now the focus, he says.

“We’ve got this great logo of a person holding a wine bottle, and for the first 25 years of the company, we were very laser-focused on the wine bottle and how we show everyone the most bottles of wine we can,” he says. “And now we’re focused on the person holding the wine bottle.”

Pinho says that shift is crucial at a time when the wine industry is struggling to connect to U.S. consumers. “The industry had a great run up over the last 25 years,” he says. “For the most part, wine was selling itself, and now what we’re all doing is taking a step back and saying, what do the customers want? How do we build longer term customers? How do we get people excited to drink wine and to consume it and to try different things?

“A lot of what we’re doing is built around using technology and using what I’ll call basic customer needs to start bridging that gap,” he continues. “I think the big benefit I have of coming into this business was that I spent 20 years as a consumer of wine and a buyer of wine, and so I had insights into what people are looking for in their buying experience and their relationship and their journey. A lot of folks that are in the wine industry started in the wine industry and they’ve only known the wine industry. I find it unusual that I’m one of the few people that actually spent a bunch of money on wine before joining.”
Big Fixes

Pinho has a multi-pronged strategy that he believes will right-size the offering and enhance margins and customer satisfaction. The first focus is to “fix pricing” so that it makes sense in today’s marketplace.

For much of its existence, Wine.com focused on selling a broad range of wines, utilizing lower-priced wines to drive volume and higher-priced wines to drive profitability. That strategy was “deteriorating the value of the higher-end proposition,” he says.

“We’re shifting pricing to be more cohesive around [meeting the needs of] folks that are spending more time and money around wine,” he continues. “We’re looking at what price is enticing them and how [we achieve] the right price mix. We’re using technology to do that.”
To that end, Wine.com has shed most of its inventory of wines priced below $15 a 750-ml., giving up volume to focus on wines that deliver higher margins.

“The second thing we’re doing is focusing on customer convenience,” Pinho says. Again using a technology solution, Wine.com is addressing customer needs for storage and timed delivery so they can take advantage of deals but not have to deal with multiple deliveries or interactions. The service mimics that which consumers expect in a local wine shop. Those stores “can deliver whenever the customer wants and it’s a much easier consumer experience,” he notes.

“Our belief is that the easier we make this for the customer, the more likely they are to spend more time with us,” Pinho adds. Another initiative launching in summer 2026 is a wine-finding service. Instead of simply selling the wines the company has in stock, Wine.com will source a wine requested by a consumer. “What we’re really trying to do is partner with the producers, partner with the wholesalers to make all that inventory available to folks as they’re looking, versus what happens to be on our live or virtual shelves on any given day of the week,” he says.

The goal, according to Pinho, is to utilize technology to streamline and optimize the purchasing process for consumers. “If customers are buying $20 wines or buying $120 wines, they get that same white glove service in terms of convenience, access, and storage,” he says, noting that storage will be free if the individual takes delivery any time from purchase up to the next “shipping window,” which will occur twice a year.
Online Presence, Live Events

Wine.com is also pushing more interactions with customers. The company utilizes both email and social media to bring new and existing customers to its site. It’s also expanding the website to include more marketing and educational messaging from suppliers, and is even co-hosting live events in select markets. “If Wilson Daniels, for example, is doing a tasting in Florida, we can figure out who their customers are or who their customers should be,” he says, noting that Wine.com can promote events to a curated list of customers.

Storytelling is also top of mind for Pinho, who says the Wine.com site is set to become more robust. “One of the things that we’re very clear about is that Wine.com is excellent at communicating with customers and providing information and the opportunity to buy wine,” he says. “But, in reality, I could never tell the story of a bottle of wine as well as the producer could, or even the distributors because they’re doing it every day. One thing we’re trying to do from a content perspective is give use of our platform to let people leverage their story more. Over the next 12 months, we’re introducing a lot of new features. Our website [will look] more like a storytelling board than it does like an e-commerce site.”

Pinho says Wine.com will encourage producers to provide videos and other promotional content for the site to entice consumers. “With technology where it is, it’s super important to let folks tap those resources when they want. We want to partner with the industry to better tell those stories, because the natural storytellers are sitting on vineyards, they’re not sitting on servers or e-com sites trying to convince people to do things.” Such efforts don’t just drive immediate sales, they provide valued data that can be shared with producers, he adds.

The efforts “reduce the barriers for consumers to discover, for consumers to explore, and for consumers to transact in ways that are easy for them,” Pinho continues. That’s crucial at a time when consumer habits are changing rapidly amidst “an invigorating time” in the industry. Pinho maintains that “younger consumers are spending just fine on the wine category, they’re just doing it a bit differently.”

“What we’re seeing from our younger customers are their frequency is similar, their spend per bottle is higher, their volume purchasing is lower,” he says, pointing to a unique “discovery pattern” among younger generations of consumers. “I think the wine discovery for younger folks is much more diversified, whereas Boomers have a heavy purchase concentration in a couple of spots in France, Bordeaux, maybe a little Italy,” Pinho adds. “Our younger consumers are all over the place, and interestingly, they’re going for better scores. They’re also not afraid to spend more on a bottle of wine.”

Those younger consumers want information and personalization, which—utilizing data—is something Wine.com can provide better than any local shop, Pinho adds. “Our ability to tell the story is really enhanced,” he says. “We can provide content and we can do some curation. We’re also doing a lot of personalization for customers now. What we’re trying to do is to fill in the gaps [with information that you] don’t find by just walking into a bottle shop.”
Category and Pricing Trends

When Pinho took over as CEO, one strategy was to cull lower-priced wines from the portfolio, instead focusing on the super-premium and luxury tiers. Now, the online retailer carries around 20,000 wine SKUs, shipped to customers from six different facilities across the U.S.

Pinho says the strategy to largely eliminate lower-priced wines is still solid despite the current economic volatility that is curbing consumption across all categories. “Wines between $20 and $40 don’t seem to be pacing any differently than above $40 in terms of what we’re seeing demand wise,” he says. “Our high-end bottle sales doing great. Things that are over $100 receive plenty of bids as people continuing to try new things. The price sensitivity is where producers or suppliers have taken a lot of price [increase] over the last three or four years. They’re selling less, at least with us.” He adds that wines whose scores from wine-tasting experts don’t match their prices are also struggling. Producers are also learning higher-end pricing limits, he says. “Interestingly enough, Bordeaux is doing great for us, and that’s been going on for more than a year,” Pinho says. “The Bordelaise have adjusted some of their pricing and [made other changes], and that’s really provided some tailwinds.” Napa wine producers are now feeling some of the same backlash Bordeaux producers went through several years ago, with pricing not in sync with demand. Wine.com is also seeing increased demand for white wines as producers are shifting the spotlight to once-sidelined offerings. And wines from Spain and Portugal are resonating. “The combination of quality and pricing is terrific,” Pinho says. At the luxury end of the pricing spectrum, “Burgundy continues to run unabated in terms of demand for hard-to-find bottles,” although Loire Valley wines are stealing some share, he adds.

Beyond wine, Wine.com carries a small selection of spirits but due to shipping restrictions, spirits account for less than 5% of revenue. “What we’re trying to do now is curate the spirits business to be more focused on the higher-end consumer,” Pinho says, noting a focus on hard-to-find labels.
Looking Ahead

Wine.com is in the midst of its evolution under new leadership, but Pinho says the ultimate goal is to improve on all metrics. “For many years we’ve been successful without necessarily building all the things that customers need, and now as we’re slowly building toward what they’re asking for and what they need to grow with us, it’s turned into incremental growth for us,” he says. “That tells me folks are looking for these solutions. There aren’t many folks that are our size that can invest behind creating that customer experience, so if we can continue to be the leader, continue to evolve, continue to give folks an easy place to find what they’re looking for,” we’re going to be able to do better than the industry.

“People want access to information—they want the ability to figure things out quickly,” he continues. “What we’re trying to do is give them tools to make that shopping consideration much easier and faster. Are they learning about wine? Are they exploring? For young collectors, are they finding it easy to figure out which wines to invest in? These are all things that we’re building tools for. The game we’re playing is, can we be better tomorrow than we are today?”

anuj-mittal.text: The first Zipps Liquor store, launched in 1994 in Houston, “was born out of a real estate problem,” according to Anuj Mittal, the now chief operating officer of the 38-store Texas chain. Mittal was a child at the time, but it was his family members who, upon settling in the United States from India, needed a start in business. “Zipps was a good base, a starting ground,” Mittal says. “From there, they really diversified into what were at that time the core businesses, which were Subways (restaurants), gas stations and retail strip centers.”

Today, Zipps is far more than a real estate solution for Midway Group, the investment firm owned by Mittal’s family. The group was founded by four family members—Nick Mittal, Mike Mittal, Paul Singh, and Bob Ghuman—who are today joined by the second generation of co-owners that includes Mittal as well as Varun Mittal, Hartej Singh, and Mansher Ghuman. Mittal works with his uncle, Mike, who serves as CEO of Zipps. The elder Mittal is widely regarded within the company as the founder and driving force behind the brand, as well as Anuj’s primary mentor. He remains directly involved in the business day-to-day, with a particular focus on margin discipline.

The 38-store Zipps Liquor chain is positioned as an inviting alternative to the big box stores and small, specialty beverage alcohol retailers. “We are the Trader Joe’s or Aldi’s of the liquor world,” Mittal says.
For his efforts to continue his family’s legacy and growing the Zipps brand as a standalone, Anuj Mittal has been named a 2026 Market Watch Leader.
Liquor Store Evolution

In the early 2000s, Zipps was still a sideline business for Midway Group. The partners frequently had vacant retail spaces adjacent to their gas stations and strip centers, and began placing Zipps stores into those spaces to fill them.

Mittal says Zipps was not a key focus for his family’s firm until around 2015, when the partners committed full resources to growing Zipps as a standalone business. At that time, the chain comprised eight stores. During the most aggressive growth years the company opened six to eight new stores annually; roughly 70% of the chain was built ground-up, with a smaller number of acquisitions.

Mittal had joined Midway Group in 2013, fresh out of the University of Houston, where he studied finance. “My first two to three years at Midway was really learning our core businesses, which at that time were the Subways and convenience stores/gas stations,” he recalls, noting that through Subway he learned how to “control the controllable numbers” like food costs and labor, and through the gas stations, learned the importance of transaction speed.

Mittal was vice president of operations when the rapid expansion began. “That’s really where my learning came from, especially those first few years where we were scaling at six to eight new stores a year,” he says. “A lot of my time was spent on creating the systems and processes that hold our team accountable to deliver that same operational excellence that we did at eight stores. Taking Zipps from eight stores to 38 in a relatively short amount of time has been a really good challenge.”

Today, Zipps Liquors has stores in the Houston metropolitan areas and in the more sparsely populated East Texas region. Combined, the 38 locations generated more than $50 million in revenue in 2025 and “we’re projecting close to the same, if not a bit more, this year,” Mittal says.

“We don’t try to be like the big box guys, and we’re certainly not the neighborhood stores,” he continues. “We’re kind of in that middle ground. Aldi and Trader Joe’s are extremely convenient. They’re not too expensive. And their selection, while it’s not huge, it’s the stuff that people are looking for. And that’s really what we are about.”

The company builds on three pillars—pricing, selection, and convenience. “In the urban areas we know we can’t beat the big guys on price and selection, but we often find that for convenience sake, people do come to us,” Mittal says. “In East Texas, in rural locations or small towns, we’re winning on all three. We are definitely the price leader and often the selection leader. And we’re definitely not less convenient than any of the other options that people have.”
The Experience

Zipps Liquor stores measure anywhere from 2,000–6,000 square feet, somewhat diminutive compared to other prominent Texas chains. They’re on the smaller side by design, Mittal says. “One of the guiding philosophies in our merchandising is that we believe any customer should be able to walk into Zipps and be able to find what they’re looking for within 30 seconds,” he says.

“Our stores are very clearly labeled—you can find the category you want to shop very easily,” he continues. “And, while this almost seems to go against normal retail knowledge, we have very low shelves in most of our stores. Our shelves are only three feet high in the middle of the store, while the wall shelves are six or seven feet high.” The reason? Higher shelves make the areas feel closed off and limit the scope customers can see at any given time.

“Plus, I think a big differentiator for Zipps is our people,” Mittal says. “Our longest tenured employees have been with us for 15 years, and more than 30% of our staff have been here for over five years.” Small, thoughtful moments—like putting a customer’s standard purchase on the counter when they enter the store, offering (but not pushing) help in-store and loading a car with a large purchase—all make a difference in the minds of customers, Mittal maintains.
“It’s a small-town, owner-operator feel in our store, but not the often-high prices you see in small, neighborhood stores,” he says.
A Varied Selection

Within those stores, Mittal says the idea is to be a “jack-of-all-trades” when it comes to selection. That doesn’t mean a massive number of SKUs. Instead, Zipps Liquor has good representation in all categories but doesn’t specialize in a single sector. That said, about 80% of the selection and sales are in spirits. An average store carries just over 2,000 SKUs, with spirits accounting for 1,700–1,800 of that total.

“We’re very picky and choosy about what we bring into our stores,” he says. “Unless we fully believe that a customer is going to like a product and they’re going to like the price point, we don’t carry the product.”

Currently, Tequila is “a rocket ship of a category” that is driving much of the sales volume. “Even Bourbon drinkers have switched to Tequila,” Mittal says, noting that Don Julio “is the king right now.” In fact, Mittal says the Don Julio 70th Anniversary Crystal Añejo Tequila, which retails for $80 at Zipps, has taken off. “A lot of our customers find that that is the closest thing to a Don Julio 1942 for them at a price point that works for them,” he says.

Wine accounts for 10–15% of volume at Zipps, and the typical mix is 150–200 SKUs, mainly core national brands. “We know our customers aren’t coming to Zipps to look for boutique wines,” Mittal says. “The bulk of our selection is concentrated on the $10 to $20 range with a few premium options mixed in.”

Beer is even less of a focus. “We don’t really actively manage our beer category,” Mittal admits. “We’re quite heavily reliant on our local beer suppliers to let us know the top SKUs we need to be carrying.” Beer demands vary based on location, so each store has a different mix, he adds.

RTDs are growing in popularity, eclipsing beer in most stores. High Noon, Cutwater and Surfside dominate, Mittal says, and Crown Royal’s RTD line is performing well. In addition, a newcomer on the scene, El Jimador’s New Mix, is “going absolutely bananas” in Zipps Liquor stores.

With limited space and SKUs, Mittal says it’s crucial for him and his team to keep abreast of any trending products. “We’re finding that we have to be tuned in on what’s happening on social media,” he says. “And we have to very quickly decide whether the hype is real or not. Is it going to die in two weeks? Are our suppliers seeing the same thing—are they having trouble stocking that item? We have to quickly make those decisions and jump on those trains, or decide not to jump on those trains.”

The Cutwater RTDs are a good example. “We had three feet of shelf space dedicated to Cutwater, but after the social media craziness that happened to them last year, we probably had 15–20 feet of our space dedicated to the brand, and the space was very, very deserved.” A similar phenomenon happened with Taylor Port, albeit on a smaller scale, a few years ago, he adds.

Zipps launched its e-commerce platform in 2022. Customers can order from any location for pickup or delivery at the same prices offered in-store, a deliberate pricing transparency commitment. Mittal says that while Zipps continues to invest in digital, leadership is explicit that the in-store experience remains the heart of the brand.
The company also maintains an active customer email program, engaging a list of more than 12,000 subscribers on a weekly basis with product launches, tastings, and store events.

The more interactive and entertaining, the better. “We’re not just looking for someone just to pour things,” he says. “We’re looking for how that tasting can deliver a better experience to our customers. What’s something that’s going to make that customer talk about their experience here at Zipps?”
Next Moves

The current economic instability, inflationary pressures and the reality that many people are drinking less or not at all, are all weighing on Zipps as an organization. “The outlook is bleak and we’re feeling it,” Mittal says. “However, due to our cost structure, we run a very lean, mean machine. We own most of our real estate. Our CEO is laser focused on margins. So, yes, the industry is down but Zipps is in a good place. We’re not in any sort of panic mode.”
In fact, Zipps is continuing its acquisition push. “Our plan is 10%-20% growth every year through acquisitions,”

Mittal says. “We’re opportunistic. This year, for example, we’re not for sure that there are going to be three or four acquisitions on the horizon, but we’re always open to if an opportunity comes up.”

“It’s really all about timing for acquisitions for us and really what works for our trade area,” he continues. “We really like for each store to be within one hour of the next store, just so that it’s a little bit easier for our team to manage.”

Mittal isn’t ruling out opportunities in other states but says Zipps is focused on Texas for now. And with the challenging landscape for beverage alcohol sales currently, he’s expecting expansion. “Even in a downturn there are opportunities,” he says. “And that’s really what we’re about.”
