adam-acquistapace.text: The Acquistapace family has a long and storied history in Louisiana retail, dating back more than 150 years. The family legacy began in the grocery sector in the 1860s and evolved to add wine and spirits retail at the end of Prohibition, and beverage alcohol is now a key component of this multi-faceted business. The family’s three stores in Louisiana’s Northshore, across Lake Pontchartrain from New Orleans, combine the feel of a neighborhood grocer with the high-end product assortment of a fine wine and spirits shop, and the Acquistapaces make sure both of those pieces work together to create a complete shopping experience.

Creative marketing and merchandising have been key tools in the family’s business arsenal for decades. The Acquistapaces originally added wine to their grocery stores to encourage shoppers to buy meat—their grocery specialty—and over the years they’ve furthered their commitment to beverage by merchandising wine and spirits with a variety of other products, from cheese to produce. “Our strategy is to have a world class fine wine and spirits store inside a grocery store,” says manager Adam Acquistapace. “Wine and spirits are part of our traffic-generating strategy and of our identity. We’ve invested a lot of time and resources into building this selection of products—we have wine from all over the world and we price it right.”
For his creative take on marketing, merchandising, and community outreach, 2018 Market Watch Leader Adam Acquistapace earns this year’s Market Watch Leaders Best Marketing Award.
A Family Legacy

Adam and his brother Erik grew up in the family business, as did their father Steve, whose parents opened a neighborhood supermarket in 1963 along the Northshore of Lake Pontchartrain. Steve opened his own store nearby in Covington, Louisiana—where the flagship is still located— in 1985. Louisiana has unrestrictive laws for beverage retail, and grocery stores throughout the state sell wine and spirits. Adam notes that his family’s stores have sold beverage alcohol since the 1930s, but they made a real commitment to the sector in 1999 when Steve changed his store’s layout so that wine could be more prominent. Adam began managing the beverage alcohol department in 2003 and now acts as general manager of the entire family business. Erik runs the cheese department, another crucial and deep section of the company’s grocery business, and he also oversees perishable goods, among other areas. Steve is all but retired, though he still comes into the stores daily. All three Acquistapaces were named 2018 Market Watch Leaders.

“When I took over the wine department, I didn’t know anything about wine,” Adam recalls. “My dad said I had to learn about business and become an expert in something. I took two years to learn about wine and spirits and got involved with the Society of Wine Educators. I now encourage and incentivize our staff to read the materials for the Certified Specialist of Wine and Spirits (CSW and CSS) and take the certification tests. My brother is a cheese professional and I took the wine path.”

Today, the family owns three stores, with a fourth in the works to open next year. Acquistapace’s Covington Supermarket, the flagship location, is currently the biggest, spanning 30,000 square feet and stocking a wide assortment of grocery and beverage items. Adam describes it as a supermarket with “cool stuff from all over the world” and adds that it’s a neighborhood grocery store with a cavern of wine and spirits inside. The beverage department has products stacked to the ceiling.

The family added the 8,000-square-foot Mandeville Wine & Cheese store in 2016 and the 15,000-square-foot Slidell Wine Warehouse in 2019, both also in Louisiana’s Northshore. Adam likens Mandeville to a high-end fine wine shop but adds that it’s also a convenience location due to its position near the foot of the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway. Meanwhile, Slidell is more of a big-box model with a massive array of beverage products and a sales strategy that emphasizes low prices. Both stores make a big commitment to the drinks side of the business but also offer the company’s key grocery items, including fresh meat and cheese. Company-wide, the Acquistapace stores carry about 10,000 wine, spirits, and beer SKUs, though the product assortment varies by location. The family declines to release revenue figures but says that beverage alcohol makes up about 30% of total sales. Of that, wine leads the drinks business at 60% of sales, followed by spirits at 30% and beer at 10%.

When the Acquistapace’s fourth unit opens next year, also in the Northshore, Louisiana market, it will be the family’s most ambitious location by far. Adam says the new store will span 75,000 square feet, including a full grocery store space and upwards of 25,000 square feet for wine, spirits, beer, and RTDs, making it the largest beverage footprint company-wide.

“We want our growth to be sustainable—we’re not growing just to grow,” Adam says. “The fine wine shop inside of a grocery store is a more sustainable model for us than a standalone wine shop. Each store has a different selection—some of it is market-driven and some of it is driven by customers.”
Customer Connection

Acquistapace’s Covington Supermarket was built as a neighborhood store and that mentality remains vital to the company’s ethos. Much of the family’s marketing tactics revolve around community events and involvement, with the overall goal to be a good neighbor and supportive local partner. Events that invite people into the stores are paramount, and the company hosts themed events regularly as part of its marketing initiatives. One of the biggest, Acquistapace’s Cheese Extravaganza, is a highlight.

The Cheese Extravaganza, which Adam’s brother Erik was instrumental in creating, is a free event that takes place every fall at the Covington store to highlight its assortment of more than 600 cheeses. The weekend event is designed to invite people in and Adam says between 8,000 and 10,000 guests usually attend. Cheese samples are available and wine and spirits are frequently featured. “We shut the store down and celebrate cheese,” Adam says. “The event has won national marketing awards in the grocery industry and we’re in the Guinness World Records for the world’s largest cheese carving. When it comes to events, you can’t pay attention to the money. We do this for our image. It creates excitement, elevates us, and enhances customer experience.” Themed events are frequent across the Acquistapace stores. The company hosts a Tasting Europe event in the spring, in which it highlights many of its European grocery and wine items and offers samples for free, and it hosts a tasting event around the start of each school year that allows parents to celebrate their kids returning to the classroom. In early summer, the stores host Tasting Local, an event that showcases products from local producers and purveyors in the stores. The family’s Covington, Louisiana store also has an adjacent event space for hosting themed classes, tastings, and special functions. Near Mardi Gras in February the company becomes a King Cake destination, as it partners with local bakeries to sell the popular cakes throughout its stores, and near Thanksgiving its sells Cajun fried turkeys, another local seasonal specialty that’s highly sought after.

“We’re trying to create excitement in a way that other stores don’t,” Adam says. “We’re a champion for other small family businesses and we focus on creating community. We look at ourselves as the town square of our area and we want to be known for that. We want people walking through our stores. We’re not a big store but we do a lot of really cool stuff.”

The Acquistapaces also partner with the local television station WWL-TV for a segment called “Great Day Louisiana,” and Adam has been a regular guest for two years. He’s featured on two segments—Happiest Hour, during which he promotes wine and food, and The Acquistapace’s Kitchen, where he works with local restaurants, chefs, and mixologists to create food and drinks and share both culinary and bar tips. This marketing strategy has vastly expanded the family’s reach and notoriety within the Northshore, Louisiana market.

The company also supports local non-profits by supplying wine and spirits for events and for charity auctions, and it helps raise money for local groups that help at-risk populations near their stores. “When we get allocations of rare whiskies, we donate most of it to non-profits for them to auction off,” Adam says. It’s important for us to be engrained into other local businesses and our towns.”
Product Assortment

Wine leads drinks sales at Acquistapace stores by a wide margin—60% of total beverage sales and roughly 6,600 SKUs. The company’s top-sellers include Bonanza Cabernet Sauvignon ($17 a 750-ml.), Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label ($54), and La Marca Prosecco ($14). Adam says consumers are showing increased interest in white wines recently, and he adds that rosés and well-priced sparkling labels are also doing well. His stores focus on French and Italian labels because that’s where Adam’s personal interest lies, especially wines from Italy.

“We’re over-indexed on French and Italian wine because we like it,” Adam says. We’re always going to champion fine wine and family-owned estates and distilleries. That’s where the business is going to continue to go.”

In spirits, whisk(e)y continues to excel and Tequila remains popular, Adam says. Whiskies produced by Sazerac generate the most buzz and Adam notes that people are also showing interest in heritage distillers like Heaven Hill and Jim Beam. Spirits comprise 30% of drinks sales and the company has about 2,500 spirits SKUs. Top-sellers include Buffalo Trace ($24 a 750-ml.), Tito’s vodka ($32 a 1.75-liter), and Jack Daniel’s ($39 a 1.75-liter).

Beer is a smaller player at 10% of drinks sales, and RTDs and THC beverages are taking up share in the segment. With about 800 beer SKUs, Adam says Mexican brews and local craft players move well. Top-selling beers include Michelob Ultra ($28 a 24-pack of cans), Gnarly Barley Jucifer ($20), and Coor’s Light ($25).

Louisiana doesn’t allow private label products, as state law mandates that every brand sold must be available to every retailer on the same terms. By that metric, Acquistapace doesn’t offer proprietary or exclusive labels. But Adam says his stores are often the only retailers locally to carry certain products, especially Bordeaux and other French labels, and he calls that a strategic part of the business.

The company’s grocer and beverage business model is helping it navigate tough times. “Our business model is very resilient to change because it’s diversified,” Adam explains, adding that being a family business also helps the bottom line. “It’s hard to separate family from business. There’s advantages to a family business, the biggest being longevity, sustainability, and continuity.”

Going forward, with growth on the horizon and change always looming, the Acquistapaces plan to focus on what they do best—making their stores a destination for local shoppers and helping the community. “We want people to feel comfortable in our stores—hospitality and service are very important,” Adam says. “Celebrating food and wine and spirits under the same umbrella is also important and we’re going to continue to focus on putting them together.”

stew-leonard.text: Stew Leonard Jr. is the renowned president and CEO of a well-respected, third-generation-managed chain of upscale grocery stores in the Northeast, a familiar voice on the radio from his commercials, who seamlessly expanded into wine and spirits retailing more than 25 years ago. While he’s earned numerous accolades for his business acumen and customer service, he’s most proud of his efforts to ensure water safety for children. The cause is dear to him—born out of personal tragedy—and ongoing as Leonard envisions widening his efforts and contributions in the years to come.

Leonard and his wife, Kim, created the Stew Leonard III Water Safety Foundation in 1990 to raise funds for water safety awareness and education initiatives following the loss of their son Stewie in a drowning accident the year prior. Stewie was just 21 months old. In addition to the foundation, the Leonards have authored a children’s book, “Stewie the Duck Learns to Swim,” to reinforce the importance of water safety, and most recently have opened two non-profit swimming schools, proceeds of which provide free or low-cost swim lessons for children in need. To date, more than $8 million has been raised for the cause.
For his compassion and generosity of spirit, Stew Leonard Jr. is the recipient of the 2026 Market Watch Leaders Community Service Award.

Daughter Ryann Leonard Grossbard is executive director of the foundation and the Stewie the Duck Swim Schools. Along with her three sisters, Grossbard says that she has been involved with the foundation “one way or another for my whole life.” She credits her parents for moving beyond their own pain to ensure that other parents don’t suffer the same fate. “It feels good to be doing something where you know you’re making a difference,” she says.

From its modest beginnings, the foundation has increasingly spread its message over the years so that communities across the U.S. have adopted “Stewie the Duck” as an educational tool for awareness and drowning prevention programs. The foundation’s annual golf tournament—held in the Connecticut/New York/New Jersey area—has been its biggest fundraiser and proceeds have been on the rise. “The first golf tournament was 29 years ago,” says Grossbard, “and we raised $800. This year, thanks to our partners, we raised over $600,000.”

Beverage alcohol suppliers and distributors have roundly supported the tournament, Stew Leonard notes, for which he is thankful. In fact, at this year’s tourney, combined contributions from beverage alcohol companies exceeded that of food companies. The retailer is also grateful that his four daughters—Ryann; Blake, president of Stew Leonard’s Wine & Spirits; Chase, creative and brand strategy director at Stew Leonard’s Farm Fresh Foods; and Madison—all serve on the foundation’s board. “It’s nice that all of our family has been able to focus on this cause,” he says. “It was all created because of their brother, and that makes it very special.”

Three years ago, the first Stewie the Duck swim school opened in Norwalk, Connecticut, home to Stew Leonard’s headquarters. Last year, a second swim school opened in Clifton, New Jersey, site of another Stew Leonard’s market. “The swim schools are non-profit so every dollar that we make is put into the foundation,” explains Grossbard, which then provides the funds for lessons given in partnership with organizations in the tri-state area. “Before the opening of the swim schools, we were preaching water safety to parents,” says Leonard. “With the schools, we’re teaching kids to swim.” Indeed, to date, more than 300,000 swim lessons have been donated thanks to net profits from the swim schools and donations to the foundation.

Stew’s wife, Kim, says, “In the last three years, the two Stewie the Duck swim schools have each taught about 1,000 lessons every week, providing 40,000 swim lessons to children who otherwise would not have had access to swim lessons, and 150 young adults instructors have been certified through the Red Cross for lifeguard training.” She and her husband plan to keep the momentum going. “We hope to open more swim schools,” says Stew Leonard. “We’d like to have a dozen of them.” But Kim adds, “why stop at 12? I’m hoping there are other swim safety foundations who would love to open a Stewie the Duck swim school. What a wonderful way to keep growing. For every child who takes a swim lesson, another child receives a lesson.”

Stew Leonard’s was founded by Stew Leonard Sr. in 1969 as a single store in Norwalk. In 1987, Leonard, Jr., took over as president and CEO and quickly grew the company into a chain of eight groceries in Connecticut, New York, and New Jersey. In 1999, he founded Stew Leonard’s Wines & Spirits, which today is comprised of eight independently owned and operated stores (the two New Jersey locations are within the grocery stores). Leonard was named a Market Watch Leader in 2010; received the Leaders Best Merchandising award in 2015; and in 2017 was named Retailer of the Year. Total annual sales revenue is estimated at $600 million, including about $100 million from the beverage alcohol stores. According to Stew Leonard’s Wine & Spirits president Blake Leonard, herself a 2021 Market Watch Leader, wine accounts for 58% of the company’s beverage alcohol sales, followed by spirits at 35%, and beer at 7%. With changing consumption habits and inflation these days, she says, “We’re seeing shifting in the cart itself. Some people are putting one less bottle into their shopping cart. But we’re also seeing some putting something else in instead.” In the company’s Connecticut and New Jersey stores, for example, that’s often THC beverages, the retailer notes.

Stew Leonard’s Wines & Spirits offers about 2,500 wine SKUs. According to Blake, a certified sommelier, “value matters more than ever right now.” One of the biggest trends she’s seeing within the wine category today is the emergence of “alternative white wines,” she says. “Consumers are increasingly intrigued by Sancerre, Vermentino, Albariño, and Vinho Verde, even if they’re a little lower in alcohol.”

The stores stock about 1,000 spirits SKUs. Among categories, Tequila and ready-to-drink (RTD) brands are performing best, Blake says. Within Tequila, “what’s really interesting is that half of all sales now come from brands with no additives,” she says. “So many customers are now asking for clean brands,” such as Lalo ($38 a 750-ml. in Norwalk). In addition, Reposado sales “continue to grow,” Blake says. “Reposado is like an introduction to drinking Bourbon.”

RTDs, meanwhile, have become “a huge part of the business,” she says. “They’re all about convenience.” Top sellers include High Noon, Surfside, and Sun Cruiser (each $30 a 12-pack of 12-ounce cans). Blake is impressed by the improved quality of the RTD category in recent years, calling out products like Via Carota craft cocktails ($22 a 375-ml.) Stew Leonard’s stocks up to 800 beer SKUs. While beer sales have been on the decline nationally, Blake says her stores have been seeing more stability lately, particularly with craft brews. However, like wine, beer sales may be negatively impacted by the proliferation of THC drinks, the retailer believes. “For some of our customers who would typically have a glass of wine a night, we’re seeing them opting to have a THC beverage maybe once or twice a week instead,” she explains. (Stew Leonard’s sells the products in its Connecticut and New Jersey stores.) But in some cases, the substitution is a boon for the stores. Blake notes that a 4-pack of THC seltzers can retail for $16. “So for customers making the shift from beer to THC, they’re not necessarily spending less.”

Change is also on the radar for Stew Leonard’s. Stew confirms that a corporate succession plan is in place—Blake will serve as president of the company and her cousin Jake Tavello, currently COO, will become CEO when Stew retires in the next few years. “The transition will take time,” he says. “I’m not going to disappear.”

Stew Leonard also sees store expansion ahead. “It’s grow or die,” he says, noting that the company is actively interested in new locations. He’s not just eyeing growth for financial reasons but for the benefit of store employees. “New stores provide growth opportunities for our team members,” the retailer says. “To attract the best and the brightest, we must provide opportunity for growth.”

Beverage alcohol will play a big role in expansion plans at the chain. Stew and Blake both point to the opportunities the Garden State provides. “We especially love New Jersey because we can sell food and wine together,” Stew says.

Business aside, he’s grateful for the bonds he’s built with industry members over the years, many of whom have supported the Stew Leonard III Water Safety Foundation. “It’s a wonderful industry,” Leonard says. “We’ve made some true friends in wine and spirits.”

best-new-products.text: Gran Malo, a tamarind-flavored Tequila liqueur from Gallo, is spicing up the premium Tequila space. The brand, which launched in Mexico in 2021 and was followed by a U.S. launch in California in 2024, has been catching fire in the States, rocketing to 360,000 cases in 2025, according to Impact Databank. Gran Malo is geared toward shot-taking occasions, offering flavors including Churro and Jamaica, among others.

“Gran Malo, which entered our portfolio last year, was the No-1 spirits growth item in California,” Gallo chief commercial officer Britt West told Market Watch sister publication Shanken News Daily (SND) in an interview earlier this year. “It now represents over 50% of all flavored Tequila and it drove 60% of dollar growth in Tequila last year. And there is more runway.”

The Tequila-based liqueur, which retails for $20 a 750-ml. and $2 a 50-ml. and comes in at 30% abv, made Market Watch’s Hot Brands list for the first time in 2025. Its growth has skyrocketed since its initial launch in Southern California in 2024. Since then, Gallo has expanded Gran Malo into several other markets across western America including Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, California, and Texas, among others. Gallo’s West noted in an interview with SND that Gran Malo has “a highly focused Mexican-American consumer, and therefore you can very effectively use data, use targeted retailers, and focus in.”

The wine world has been adapting to broad new industry trends as consumers—particularly younger legal-drinking-age ones—have been seeking out healthier drinking options. Decoy, part of the Duckhorn portfolio, is one of many all-star brands that has leaned into the better-for-you wine segment with the release of Decoy Featherweight, a low-calorie and low-abv line of wines designed to introduce the Decoy brand to “a new audience of consumers who are engaging with wine on different occasions and in different ways,” Duckhorn’s then-interim president, CEO, and chairperson Deirdre Mahlan said at the line’s 2024 launch.

Decoy Featherweight released its first wine, a Sauvignon Blanc, in January of 2024, followed by a Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay in 2025. Each wine has just 80 calories and clocks in at 9% abv, meeting health-minded consumers exactly where they want to be. The line depleted 63,000 9-liter cases last year, according to Impact Databank.

Decoy Featherweight is available nationally and is priced intentionally at $20 a 750-ml., a price segment that Decoy has been trying to break into, according to Chanel Caplan, senior vice president of premium brands at Duckhorn. “We made the decision about a year ago to strategically reposition the pricing to really compete in that $15–$20 segment,” Caplan told Market Watch sister publication Shanken News Daily last year.

lunazul.text: Tequila has been a strong market over the past decade, more than doubling in size from 14.6 million cases in 2015 to 31.9 million cases in 2025, according to Impact Databank. But sales dramatically slowed down last year, with the total category eking out a modest 0.5% volume increase as several top brands registered losses. Amid the slowdown, Heaven Hill’s premium-tier Lunazul kept its foot on the gas with a 29.5% volume increase. Its resilience and strong growth earns it the Market Watch Leaders Spirits Brand of the Year award.

Lunazul has been consistently growing since making its U.S. debut in 2008 through a joint venture between Heaven Hill and Tierra de Agaves, the distillery founded by Francisco Beckmann of the legendary Beckmann Tequila dynasty. The brand, which launched with a Blanco and Reposado, differentiated itself early on by offering 100% agave Tequila in the $20–$30 a 750-ml. price tier—one of the very first products of its kind to compete in this segment historically led by mixtos like Jose Cuervo, Sauza, and others. Accessibility was a main selling point, supported by early marketing positioning Lunazul as a straightforward, no-nonsense option at an approachable price. That combination made it a hit with younger consumers, with Heaven Hill identifying 25- to 35-year-olds as a key demographic. The brand began hitting its stride in the early 2010s, releasing its first Añejo in 2011 and surging past 60,000 cases with strong year-to-year growth. The majority of that business came from off-premise channels, but it also gained traction with bartenders and mixologists, who were drawn to its production methods and brand heritage. Back in 2012, Shanken News Daily spoke to longtime director of sales analysis Andy Shapira, who was very optimistic about the brand’s growth. “We were at the forefront of the 100% agave trend, and we definitely filled a space for consumers between Jose Cuervo and Patron,” he said. “We have significant distribution around the country, and I don’t see why we can’t blast through six digits [of volume] in the future.” By 2015 Shapira’s projections would come true, with Lunazul’s volume nearly doubling in a five-year period to 100,000 cases. It earned “Hot Brand” status just three years later.

The brand’s growth has been nothing short of meteoric since then. Just five years ago, Lunazul didn’t crack the top ten brands in the U.S. in terms of volume. Now it’s the No.-3 brand overall, surpassing established rival Patrón for the first time in 2025 at 2.2 million cases. The lineup also includes the Primero Collection, a higher-end series that includes the smoky Humoso, an extra añejo, as well as single-estate expressions. “Lunazul is seeing strong momentum across the entire portfolio, with growth coming from all sizes and formats,” says senior brand manager Brittany Wenig, noting that Reposado is a specific growth driver, with depletions up nearly 50% year-over-year.

As premiumization slows and consumers migrate from luxury-priced brands to more affordable options, Lunazul seems uniquely positioned to capture even more market share. Impact Databank projects the brand will see yet another year of double-digit growth in 2026.

avaline.text: Celebrity wine and spirits brands are a dime a dozen these days. What’s infinitely rarer are those that are worth their salt, delivering not just a recognizable name behind the label, but quality in the glass and savvy marketing as well. One such wine brand proving that a celebrity backing can indeed be a boon is Avaline, co-owned by actor Cameron Diaz and entrepreneur Katherine Power; for that reason, it’s been named the 2026 Market Watch Leaders Wine Brand of the Year.

Diaz and Power launched Avaline with a Spanish white wine and a Provençal rosé, both made from organic grapes, in July 2020. In the brand’s first three months on shelves, it sold 10,000 cases—a bellwether of the success to come—and by October 2020, it had added a Rhône red to the portfolio. Numerous additional wines have since joined its core stable, among them Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and a duo of sparkling wines (one white and one rosé), all of which are made with organic grapes. The entire portfolio falls within the $20–$28 a 750-ml. price range, putting it firmly in super-premium territory. In terms of bright spots within this lineup, the more recently added Prosecco has served as a particularly valuable extension for the brand—CEO Jennifer Purcell notes that in its first 30 days on market, in November 2025, it became the fastest-selling single-bottle release in Avaline’s DTC history. In the past few years, the brand has bucked trends in the greater wine space—where such conditions as increasingly health-conscious consumers and less consumption among younger drinkers have contributed to volume declines— and rapidly grown, skyrocketing from a base of 80,000 cases in 2022 to more than 300,000 cases in 2025, according to Impact Databank. Last year was an especially pivotal one for the brand, with depletions rising by nearly 50% year-over-year. At the heart of these soaring numbers is Avaline’s outside-the-box approach to brand development. “We built the brand more like a modern lifestyle company than a traditional wine label by prioritizing retail and DTC early, investing in design, and building cultural relevance beyond the wine aisle,” Purcell says.

Thus far, this has included engaging in strategic partnerships with brands including Moda Operandi, J. Crew, Anthropologie Weddings, Williams Sonoma, and Instacart, as well as releasing limited edition wines made in collaboration with various lifestyle brands (last year, for instance, saw the debut of limited-edition packaging by fashion designer Stella McCartney for Avaline’s rosé). “Limited releases have become an important part of how we introduce new consumers to the brand while keeping existing customers engaged,” Purcell notes, adding that additional limited editions were introduced over the summer.

Coming up for Avaline is a push in national retail chains. While DTC is a key contributor to the brand’s sales, it’s available in a slew of major stores as well, among them Kroger, Target, and Whole Foods. Now, it’ll arrive on shelves at more than 1,500 Kroger stores, 1,400 Target locations, and 350 Whole Foods outlets, according to senior vice president of sales Matthew Szura, setting the stage for more meteoric growth ahead.

tom-day.text: Reyes Beverage Group is a titan among U.S. beverage alcohol distributors as the country’s leading beer distributor, delivering around 320 million cases annually to over 115,000 retail accounts nationwide. Nearly all the Reyes business traditionally has been in beer—until 2023, when the company began ramping up its activity on the wine and spirits side. It all started with a 2023 deal to handle the Sazerac’s business in California and parts of Texas, and what has since followed is a series of moves into wine and spirits distribution, as Reyes added such suppliers as Gallo, Tito’s, Brown-Forman, and other major players. But its biggest move of all came this year, with an agreement to acquire the businesses of Republic National Distributing Co. (RNDC) in a deal that was finalized this past spring. RNDC had been the nation’s No.-2 spirits and wine distributor behind Southern Glazer’s Wine & Spirits, covering some 11 states including Arizona, Florida, Hawaii, Louisiana, Maryland, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, Virginia, and Washington, D.C.

The RNDC acquisition accounted for nearly $7 billion in new business for Reyes this calendar year, and made it the nation’s third-largest spirits and wine distributor behind Breakthru and Southern. The entire move has been a thunder-clap over the industry, rearranging the wine and spirits second tier in a way that was virtually unprecedented for its speed.

Leading the company’s operations through all this massive change has been Tom Day, CEO of Reyes Beverage Group since 2019. Day came to Reyes from Diageo, where he had served as global chief sales officer and chairman of the company’s US Beer Division, where he placed particular focus on digitally enabled sales. Building off the tools learned from his impressive beer pedigree, Day has been driving the wine and spirits side, hitting the ground running and laying the groundwork for future growth. And while spirits might seem to be the focus in this new diversification, Day has also emphasized that wine will be a major part of the picture. “We want to make it clear that we’re committed to wine, and the wine industry,” Day said in an interview earlier this year with Market Watch sister publication Shanken News Daily, noting that the RNDC deal won Reyes one of the largest wine distribution businesses in the country.

While beer sales at Reyes account for around 80% of the total picture for Reyes, spirits and wine have obviously grown by leaps and bounds over the past three years, with future growth still very likely. Reyes has been ramping up on its newly acquired wine and spirits activities, according to Day, adding over 1,000 commercial roles on that side of the business and investing in workshops, cocktail labs, and sales training programs to hone its expertise. Particular attention is being paid to the national accounts side and growth management, but there are also major investments in warehousing and equipment to help improve storage and delivery of inventory. As Reyes Beverage celebrates the 50th year of its founding this year, there’s been little time for celebrating as the new business becomes integrated into the company. But it’s been quite a year, with the promise of more growth to come, and CEO Tom Day will be at the center of it.
